mcq.q: Why are non-linear activations needed?
options: Without them, stacked layers collapse into one linear map
mcq.why: Compositions of linear maps are linear; non-linearity lets networks model curved boundaries.

mcq.q: A ReLU neuron has weights w = [2, −1], bias b = 0.5 and input x = [1, 3]. What does it output?
distractors: That is z before the activation; ReLU sets negatives to 0.
That adds all the products as positives.

mcq.q: ReLU's gradient is 0 for negative inputs. What practical problem can that cause?
options: Neurons whose inputs are always negative stop learning (dead ReLUs)
mcq.why: No gradient flows through a neuron that never activates, so its weights never update.
distractors: Zero gradients are the opposite of exploding.

mcq.q: Which loss is standard for classification and language modelling?
mcq.why: Cross-entropy rewards probability on the right class or token; MSE is the usual choice for regression.
distractors: Hinge loss is used by SVMs, not language models.
MAE is also a regression loss.

mcq.q: You apply softmax to the outputs and then pass them to PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss. What happens?
options: Training runs, but gradients shrink and the model learns slowly
mcq.why: CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits and applies log-softmax itself; a second softmax squashes the signal.
distractors: The double softmax changes the gradients.
It runs without error, which is why the bug is common.

mcq.q: In the worked example, ŷ = w₂·h with h = 0.5, target y = 2 and prediction ŷ = 1. With L = (ŷ − y)², what is ∂L/∂w₂?
distractors: That is ∂L/∂ŷ, before multiplying by h.

mcq.q: How is one layer of many neurons computed?
options: As one matrix multiplication (plus a bias and an activation)
One neuron at a time in a Python loop
mcq.why: Stacking each neuron's weights as rows of a matrix computes the whole layer at once.
distractors: That is far slower and not how frameworks work.

mcq.q: Why is backpropagation efficient?
options: It reuses intermediate results stored during the forward pass
It only updates the last layer
It skips most of the weights
mcq.why: Each layer's stored values let the chain rule run backward once instead of recomputing each path.
distractors: The forward pass supplies the stored values.
It computes gradients for every weight.

mcq.q: GELU and SiLU are…
options: Smooth variants of ReLU used in transformers
mcq.why: They behave like ReLU for large inputs but are smooth around zero.

mcq.q: Why are sigmoid and tanh less common in the hidden layers of deep networks?
options: They saturate, so gradients become very small for large inputs
They are too slow to compute
mcq.why: In their flat regions the derivative is near zero, which slows or stops learning in deep stacks.
distractors: Speed is not the main issue.

interview.q: Walk through a forward and backward pass for a two-layer network.
covers: Weighted sums and activations, storing intermediates
Chain rule backward through each layer
Gradient for every weight, then an update

interview.q: Why do neural networks need non-linear activations?
covers: Stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map
Only straight decision boundaries without them
Example: separating a spiral or circles

interview.q: What is the difference between logits, probabilities and the loss?
covers: Softmax or sigmoid turns them into probabilities
Loss compares probabilities with the target
Losses often take logits for numerical stability

interview.q: Your classifier trains but learns very slowly, and you find softmax applied before CrossEntropyLoss. Explain what is happening.
covers: Remove the extra softmax and recheck the first loss

interview.q: When would you choose an MLP over gradient-boosted trees for tabular data?
covers: Trees usually win on plain tabular data
MLPs help with embeddings or mixed inputs
Need for end-to-end training with other networks
Compare fairly on the same split and metric

interview.q: {company} needs to tag each product with several attributes that can all be true at once. How do you set up the output layer and loss?
Design a small guardrail classifier on top of sentence embeddings for an assistant.
covers: A small MLP head and labelled examples
Thresholds from precision and recall needs
interview.followUp: How would you keep it accurate as the assistant's traffic changes?

interview.q: Explain the cost of backpropagation compared with the forward pass, and why it matters for training budgets.
covers: Backward is roughly twice the forward compute
Activations must be stored, which costs memory
Activation checkpointing trades compute for memory

mcq.q: You call torch.no_grad() during evaluation but not model.eval(). What still happens?
mcq.why: no_grad stops gradient recording only; eval() switches dropout and normalisation to inference mode.

mcq.q: What does loss.backward() do in PyTorch?
options: Runs backpropagation and fills each parameter's .grad
mcq.why: Autograd walks the recorded graph backward; the optimiser's step() then updates the weights.
distractors: The loss is computed before backward().

mcq.q: You forget to call opt.zero_grad() each step. What happens?
options: Gradients accumulate across steps, so updates are wrong
mcq.why: PyTorch adds new gradients to existing ones by default.

mcq.q: What does requires_grad=True on a tensor mean?
options: Operations on it are recorded so gradients can be computed
It must be on a GPU
mcq.why: Autograd records a computation graph for tensors that need gradients.
distractors: Labels normally do not need gradients.

mcq.q: Why overfit one small batch before a real run?
options: It makes the final model better
If the model cannot drive loss near zero on 8 examples, there is a bug
mcq.why: Wrong labels, a wrong loss or frozen weights show up immediately.
distractors: It is a test, not a training technique.

mcq.q: Your code runs but results are wrong, and tensor shapes were never printed. What is a likely cause?
options: Silent broadcasting combined tensors of unexpected shapes
mcq.why: Broadcasting makes mismatched shapes run without error; print shapes at each step.
distractors: A fixed seed is good practice.
Too few epochs gives undertrained, not wrong, results.

mcq.q: What must a checkpoint contain to resume training exactly?
options: Model and optimiser state (and the scheduler's)
mcq.why: Without optimiser and schedule state, the resumed run behaves like a restart.
distractors: A loss value cannot restore anything.
Optimiser moments and the schedule restart without them.

mcq.q: Gradient norms are exactly zero for some layers. What does that suggest?
options: A disconnected graph or dead ReLUs
mcq.why: No gradient means no learning for those layers.
distractors: A large rate gives large, not zero, gradients.
Zero gradients mean nothing is learning there.

mcq.q: What is torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) for?
options: Finding the operation that produced a NaN, briefly, because it is slow
mcq.why: It adds checks to every operation, so enable it only while debugging.

mcq.q: Where does gradient clipping go in the training loop?
mcq.why: Gradients must exist before they can be clipped, and clipping must happen before they are applied.
distractors: Gradients from this step do not exist yet.
Too late: the weights have changed.

interview.q: Explain how autograd works in PyTorch.
covers: Operations on tensors that need gradients are recorded
No need to write backward passes

interview.q: Walk through a minimal training loop and what each line does.
What must a checkpoint contain to resume training exactly?
covers: Random states, if exact reproduction matters

interview.q: Your model cannot overfit eight examples. What do you check?
covers: Data augmentation or dropout left on
interview.followUp: What is the first line of code you would add?

interview.q: Validation numbers are noisy between runs. Which PyTorch mistakes could cause that?
covers: Dropout or BatchNorm in training mode

interview.q: {company}'s weekly retrain resumed from a checkpoint and the loss jumped. Why, and how do you fix it?
covers: Optimiser or scheduler state not saved
The learning rate restarted from warm-up
Data loader position or data changed
Save full state and test resume

interview.q: Design a training-script template your team must use for every model.
How would you debug a NaN that appears only after hours of training?
covers: Resume from the nearest checkpoint to reproduce
Inspect the batch and its data

mcq.q: A 10-class classifier's first-step loss is 2.30. This suggests…
options: a uniform starting guess, as expected
mcq.why: ln(10) ≈ 2.30 is the loss of uniform predictions, the normal starting point.

mcq.q: What goes wrong if every weight starts at zero?
options: Every neuron in a layer computes the same thing and they never learn different features
mcq.why: Identical weights get identical gradients, so the symmetry is never broken.
distractors: It does not train usefully at all.
Gradients do not explode; they are identical.

mcq.q: Xavier (Glorot) and He (Kaiming) initialisation scale the weights' variance to…
mcq.why: Scaling by fan-in or fan-out keeps activations from growing or shrinking through the layers.
distractors: Batch size does not enter the formula.

mcq.q: When do gradients vanish in early layers?
options: When the factors multiplied during backprop are mostly below 1
When the learning rate is high
mcq.why: Many small factors multiply to almost nothing, so early layers barely learn.
distractors: A high rate causes overshooting, not vanishing.
Data size is not the cause.

mcq.q: Why do transformers use LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm?
options: BatchNorm cannot be computed on GPUs
LayerNorm normalises within each example, so it does not depend on batch size
mcq.why: BatchNorm uses statistics across the batch, which is awkward for variable-length sequences and small batches.
distractors: LayerNorm has learnable scale and shift.
BatchNorm is common in CNNs for images.

mcq.q: What is RMSNorm?
options: A cheaper variant of LayerNorm used by many current LLMs
mcq.why: It rescales by the root mean square without subtracting the mean.

mcq.q: What happens to dropout at inference time?
options: It stays the same as in training
mcq.why: Dropout only regularises training; model.eval() disables it so predictions are deterministic.
distractors: Leaving it on makes predictions random.

mcq.q: The gradient norm is 5.0 and the clipping limit is 1.0. By what factor is the gradient scaled?
mcq.why: Clipping rescales the gradient to the limit: 1.0 ÷ 5.0 = 0.2.

mcq.q: Training loss falls to 2.1, jumps to 7.8 at step 14,200 and then becomes NaN. Which response matches the topic's advice?
options: Restart from scratch with a bigger model
Clip gradients, lower the peak learning rate, use BF16, inspect the offending batch and resume from a checkpoint
mcq.why: Likely causes are a too-high rate, a corrupted batch or FP16 overflow; fix the cause and resume.
distractors: A bigger model does not fix the cause.
A spike to NaN needs action.

mcq.q: A NaN is traced to one 40,000-token corrupted document. What is the best fix?
options: Filter or length-check the data, and add gradient clipping as a guard
mcq.why: The data caused it; clipping alone treats the symptom.
distractors: Fewer steps does not remove the record.
A lower rate may delay the failure, not remove the bad record.
That would make training less stable.

interview.q: What are vanishing and exploding gradients, and how do modern networks avoid them?
covers: Products of many factors in backprop

interview.q: Explain BatchNorm versus LayerNorm and when each is used.
covers: Across the batch versus across features in one example

interview.q: What does dropout do, and why is it off at inference?
covers: Off at inference for deterministic outputs

interview.q: Your loss spikes and goes NaN mid-training. Walk through your response.
covers: Stop and keep the last good checkpoint
Check data, learning rate and precision
interview.followUp: What would you log so the next spike is faster to diagnose?

interview.q: When is gradient clipping the right fix, and when does it hide a bug?
covers: Right: occasional large gradients in healthy training
Hiding: corrupted data or a wrong loss

interview.q: {company}'s image model swings in validation accuracy when fine-tuned with batches of 4. What is going on, and what would you do?
covers: BatchNorm statistics are noisy with tiny batches
Freeze the running statistics or BatchNorm layers
Use a normalisation that does not depend on batch size
Increase the effective batch where possible

interview.q: Design safeguards in a training pipeline so one bad record cannot ruin a long run.
covers: Data validation: lengths, value ranges, encodings

interview.q: {company} must explain to auditors why a monthly fraud-model run failed and was rerun. What would you record?
covers: Seeds and configuration of both runs

mcq.q: One epoch is…
options: One full pass over the training data
mcq.why: A step is one update from one batch; an epoch covers every example once.

mcq.q: With 10,000 training examples and a batch size of 32, how many steps are in one epoch?
mcq.why: 10,000 ÷ 32 = 312.5, so 313 steps including the last partial batch.
distractors: That would be a batch size of 1.

mcq.q: A run uses batch size 4 with 8 gradient-accumulation steps. What is the effective batch size?
mcq.why: Gradients from 8 batches of 4 are summed before one update: an effective batch of 32.

mcq.q: How does AdamW differ from Adam?
options: It decouples weight decay from the gradient update
mcq.why: Applying weight decay directly to the weights, separate from the adaptive step, works better in practice.
distractors: It still has a learning rate.
It stores the same two moments as Adam.

mcq.q: Why use a learning-rate warm-up at the start of training?
options: Adam's running statistics are unreliable early, so large updates can destabilise training
Because the loss is zero at first
mcq.why: Starting near zero and ramping up avoids huge early steps.
distractors: The initial loss is high, not zero.
Warm-up adds a little time; it buys stability.

mcq.q: What does momentum add to SGD?
options: A running average of gradients, so steps speed up in consistent directions
mcq.why: Velocity accumulates along steady slopes and damps oscillations across them.
distractors: Per-parameter scaling is what Adam adds.

mcq.q: Validation loss starts rising in epoch 3 while training loss keeps falling. What should you do?
options: Stop at, or keep the checkpoint from, epoch 2 (early stopping)
mcq.why: The model has begun to overfit; the epoch-2 checkpoint generalises better.
distractors: A higher rate will not cure overfitting.
Validation loss is the generalisation signal.

mcq.q: How many extra numbers per parameter does Adam store?
options: Two (the first and second moment averages)
mcq.why: That extra state is why optimiser memory matters for large models (6.6).

mcq.q: When you move to much larger batches, what usually has to change?
options: A larger learning rate, usually with warm-up
mcq.why: Smoother gradients from large batches allow, and often need, a larger step to keep progress per epoch.
distractors: Without retuning, training can be slow or unstable.

mcq.q: Memory allows a batch of only 4, but you want the effect of 64. What do you do?
options: Accumulate gradients over 16 small batches before each update
Use a batch of 4 and train 16 times longer
mcq.why: Gradient accumulation sums gradients from several small batches, simulating the larger batch.
distractors: That does not reproduce a batch of 64.
Longer training is not the same as a larger batch.

interview.q: Explain batches, steps and epochs.
covers: Epoch: one pass over the data
How they relate to time and cost

interview.q: How does Adam work, and why is it the default for transformers?
covers: Running averages of gradients and squared gradients
Robust across layers with different scales
Memory cost of two extra values per parameter

interview.q: Why use a learning-rate warm-up and decay?
You doubled the batch size and training became unstable. What do you change?

interview.q: How do you choose the number of epochs for a fine-tuning run?
{company} has only a few hundred labelled dispute cases. How do you set up optimisation to avoid overfitting?
covers: Low learning rate and few epochs
Freezing most layers or using LoRA

interview.q: Design the training configuration for fine-tuning on one GPU with limited memory.
covers: Gradient accumulation for the effective batch

interview.q: How would you run a learning-rate sweep cheaply, and decide from it?
covers: Compare validation loss after a fixed number of steps
Pick a value below where training diverges

mcq.q: What does representation learning mean?
options: The network learns useful internal vectors as a by-product of its training task
Engineers write the features by hand
mcq.why: To predict the next word well, a model must encode meaning, syntax and facts in its vectors.
distractors: Models do not store the raw text.

mcq.q: Which word2vec relationship does the topic describe?
mcq.why: Vector arithmetic can capture relations such as capital-of.
distractors: That is not the documented analogy.
That would make Rome and Italy identical.
Paris and France are related but not equal.

mcq.q: Contrastive learning trains embeddings by…
options: Minimising mean squared error on labels
Pulling matching pairs together and pushing non-matching pairs apart
mcq.why: Query–passage pairs are the positives; other passages are the negatives.
distractors: k-means does not train an encoder.

mcq.q: What are in-batch negatives?
options: The other passages in the same training batch, used as negatives
mcq.why: Each query's positive passage is a negative for every other query, so negatives come free.
distractors: There are no labels beyond the pairing.

mcq.q: Why do hard negatives help most?
options: They are similar but wrong, so the model learns fine distinctions
mcq.why: Random negatives are too easy; near-misses teach the boundaries that matter.
distractors: Ease of labelling is not the reason.
Random ones are the easy kind.
They usually make training harder, not faster.

mcq.q: How does the InfoNCE loss treat training?
options: As classification: softmax over similarities, cross-entropy with the positive as the right class
mcq.why: The positive passage should get the highest similarity among all candidates.

mcq.q: What is the difference between token embeddings and sentence embeddings?
options: Token embeddings are used for RAG search
Token embeddings are an LLM's input lookup table; sentence embeddings come from a separate model and go in a vector database
Sentence embeddings are inside every LLM's first layer
mcq.why: They are easy to confuse; RAG uses sentence or passage embeddings (chapter 9).
distractors: RAG stores passage embeddings, not token rows.
They are produced and used differently.

mcq.q: A general embedding model places “PTO” far from “annual leave”. What does the topic suggest?
options: Use a larger LLM for answers
Evaluate on your own terms, and domain-tune the embedding model if needed (13.5)
mcq.why: General models may never have seen internal acronyms; domain tuning teaches them.
distractors: Editing documents does not fix queries.
The answer model is not the retrieval problem.
Keyword search helps exact terms but does not fix the semantic gap.

mcq.q: You use an LLM's internal hidden states as search embeddings without evaluating them. What is the risk?
options: General hidden vectors are not automatically good retrieval vectors
They are always better than embedding models
mcq.why: Embedding models are trained specifically for similarity; measure before you rely on anything else.

mcq.q: Which tasks exploit embedding similarity? Choose all that apply.
mcq.why: Nearby vectors mean similar text, which powers search, grouping, duplicate detection and routing.
distractors: Arithmetic needs exact computation, not similarity.

interview.q: What is an embedding, and how is a text embedding model trained?
covers: A vector where similar meanings are close

interview.q: Explain the difference between token embeddings inside an LLM and sentence embeddings for RAG.
covers: Token embeddings: one row per vocabulary entry
Sentence embeddings: one vector per text, from a separate model
Which one goes in a vector database

interview.q: What is contrastive learning, and why do hard negatives matter?
covers: Pull positives together, push negatives apart

interview.q: Your search misses internal acronyms. How do you diagnose and fix it?
covers: Build queries with acronyms and check nearest results
Compare a general and a domain model

interview.q: How would you evaluate whether one embedding model is better than another for your corpus?
covers: Results by slice, such as language or document type

interview.q: {assistant} confuses “change date” and “cancel” requests in Hinglish. How do you improve the intent embeddings?
covers: Contrastive fine-tuning with these hard negatives
A minimum similarity and a clarifying question

interview.q: Design an embedding fine-tuning pipeline from search logs.
covers: Pairs from queries and clicked results
Deduplication and a held-out evaluation set

interview.q: What governance applies to stored embeddings of customer text?
covers: Derived from personal data, so treated like it
Retention and deletion that follow the source
Access control on the vector store

mcq.q: How does a CNN process an image?
options: It slides small learned filters across the image to detect local patterns
It attends from every pixel to every other pixel
It reads pixels one at a time with a hidden state
mcq.why: Filters detect edges, then textures, parts and objects in deeper layers.

mcq.q: Why are CNNs efficient?
options: They only look at one pixel
The same filter weights are shared across every position
mcq.why: Weight sharing means far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer over the image.

mcq.q: A 3×3 filter slides over a 6×6 image with stride 1 and no padding. What is the output size?
mcq.why: Output width = 6 − 3 + 1 = 4 in each direction.
distractors: That would need a larger filter or stride.

mcq.q: In an RNN, which weights are applied at each time step?
options: The same weights at every step
mcq.why: hₜ = f(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁) reuses W and U along the sequence.
distractors: The recurrent weights are used every step.

mcq.q: Why does information from early tokens fade in an RNN?
options: It must survive many multiplications through the hidden state
mcq.why: Repeated multiplication shrinks the signal over long spans.

mcq.q: Which gates does an LSTM use?
mcq.why: Gates learn what to keep, write and expose from the cell state.

mcq.q: What was the bottleneck in RNN sequence-to-sequence models?
options: The whole input had to fit into one fixed vector
Outputs were limited to one word
mcq.why: A single vector must carry everything about a long input.
distractors: The decoder is a trained network.

mcq.q: How did attention fix the seq2seq bottleneck?
options: The decoder weights every encoder position directly when generating each output
By using a bigger fixed vector
mcq.why: Generating “student” can focus on “étudiant”, whatever the input length.
distractors: Short inputs avoid, not fix, the problem.
A bigger vector only delays the problem.

mcq.q: Why can an RNN not be parallelised across time during training?
options: Each step needs the previous step's hidden state
mcq.why: The strict left-to-right dependency forces sequential computation.
distractors: Parameter count is not the issue.
GPUs run RNNs, just less efficiently.

mcq.q: Where do CNN-based models still commonly appear in document pipelines?
options: Layout detection and OCR before any LLM sees the text
mcq.why: Detecting tables and reading scanned text are vision tasks (10.3).
distractors: Vector stores do not use CNNs.
Token choice is the language model's decoding step.

interview.q: Explain how a CNN processes an image.
covers: Small filters slide across the image

interview.q: Why did LSTMs improve on plain RNNs, and what limits remained?
covers: Cell state and gates preserve information longer
Still sequential, so slow to train
Still forget over very long spans

interview.q: What was the seq2seq bottleneck, and how did attention fix it?
covers: One fixed vector for the whole input
Attention lets the decoder look at every encoder state
Weights depend on the current output

interview.q: Where would you still use a CNN or LSTM today instead of a transformer?
covers: When a measured comparison favours them

covers: Field extraction for amount, date, payee
Rules: amount in words matches figures, date validity
Human review below a confidence threshold

covers: Compare OCR text with the source image
Check the LLM's input versus its output
Measure OCR character error on numbers

covers: Handling busy backgrounds and new categories
